subject: history

moments.title: Watt's separate condenser patent
moments.body: Watt patents the separate condenser, a key efficiency improvement on Newcomen's atmospheric engine. Boulton's Birmingham works partners with Watt from 1775. Rotary motion (1781) allows steam to drive factory machinery, not just pumps.
moments.takeaway: Steam is just one strand. Mechanised cotton spinning (Arkwright's water frame 1769, Crompton's mule 1779) was already transforming textiles.

moments.title: First census
moments.body: Britain's first modern census records around 10.5 million people. London is the largest city in Europe at around 1 million. Manchester's population has roughly tripled since 1750.
moments.takeaway: The state begins to count its population in order to plan and tax — itself an industrial-era innovation.

moments.title: Liverpool and Manchester Railway opens
moments.body: 15 September 1830: the first inter-city passenger railway opens. William Huskisson MP is killed on the day — the first widely reported railway fatality. By 1850, Britain has around 6,000 miles of railway.

quote.text: I have lost some skin, but no breath; and my appetite remains as keen as ever.
quote.attrib: George Stephenson, on early steam locomotive trials

moments.takeaway: Railways collapse time and distance. Communication, markets and time itself are restructured.

now.title: The first industrial economy
now.body: Britain's share of world manufacturing peaked around 1870 at over 30%. The model spread to Belgium, Germany, the US, France and (later) Japan. Pat Hudson, Maxine Berg, Joel Mokyr and Robert Allen have produced competing accounts of why Britain industrialised first — cheap coal, high wages, the patent system, Enlightenment culture, empire markets.
now.open_questions: Was the Industrial Revolution a revolution or evolution? Nick Crafts's growth statistics show slow per-capita growth before 1830. The 'revolution' frame has been challenged but the structural shifts — energy, urbanisation, factory organisation — are real.

reflection: The Industrial Revolution is the most consequential event in human history after agriculture. It is also one of the slowest — perhaps a century of cumulative change rather than a moment.
